Hazards the review asked to look for, and what I found:
- "A Set-Cookie on a rewrite that could break the Expo app?" The marker is httpOnly, so the Expo bundle's JS cannot read or be confused by it; the Expo app authenticates against the API origin, not this one, so it never travels on an auth request; and it is stamped only when Accept contains text/html, so the SPA's own bundle/manifest/asset fetches (which are still proxied) never mint it — pinned by two rows.
- One-way door: once stamped, a phone that visited the app is sent back to the app at "/" for a year. The only exits are ?desktop=1 / prefer-desktop, which win over both signals — pinned by two rows. There is no "forget the marker" path; if the lead wants the marketing home reachable on a phone that has ever opened the app, that is a follow-up decision, not something I invented here.
- G (/nope on a phone -> Expo "Unmatched Route") is unchanged, as ruled ACCEPT. My asset/auth exemptions are exact prefixes/paths and do not widen into unmatched paths.

Not in scope and not touched: MARKETING_PATHS membership, the landing 307, the operator path guard, the tenant-slug cookies, config.matcher.

One-way door, wider than A3 intended. The marker is stamped on EVERY proxied phone document request, /login included — my probe P3 confirms: a first-time visitor who taps "Sign in" in the marketing chrome gets rf-mobile-app=1 for a year, after which bare `/` never serves the marketing home on that phone again. This is exactly what A3 prescribed, so it is not an executor deviation — but the lead should decide whether to skip the stamp when the proxied path is an auth entry point, or shorten the max-age.

The regate's ESLint RED is an instrument artifact, not a code defect — do not spend a round on those 46 problems. apps/web carries TWO eslint configs: `.eslintrc.json` (extends next/core-web-vitals only), which is what `next lint` resolves, and `eslint.config.mjs`, which ALSO extends next/typescript (error-level no-explicit-any / no-unused-vars) and is what the regate's root-binary invocation picks up, with --max-warnings 0 finishing the job. I ran the real CI gate: `npx next lint` in apps/web → EXIT 0, 0 errors, 58 warnings; CI runs `npm run verify` → `turbo run … lint` → `next lint`. Neither (auth)/login/page.tsx nor buyer/portal/layout.tsx produces any finding there, and customers/[id]/page.tsx has the same 16 `: any` on origin/master. The dual config itself is the hazard — worth a registry row.

Latent trap for the new tone prop: `.rf-marketing .brand-mark { mix-blend-mode: multiply }` means a tone="light" mark rendered inside the marketing cascade would multiply white ink against the cream page and disappear. No marketing call site passes tone="light" today (all four are outside .rf-marketing), so nothing is broken now — but the next person who re-tones a marketing surface will hit it. Worth one comment line next to the tone prop.

Two small-text colours in the same light-override region C1 fixed are still sub-4.5:1, just outside the ruling's named .hero-note/.lead/.eyebrow scope: `.rf-marketing .connection-nodes > div` #8298b5 and (line 5110) `.connection-diagram > p` #8b9eb8, both painted on `.connection-diagram { background: #f4f7fc }` → 2.75:1 and 2.55:1 by my WCAG snippet. Not blocking, but it is the same class of defect on the same screens and should join C1's follow-up rather than be discovered by an accessibility audit later.

`brand-mark--light` is a dead class — no CSS rule defines it anywhere (grep across globals.css and marketing.css), and the visual effect comes entirely from the Tailwind `brightness-0 invert` pair. It works today purely as a test hook, which is fine, but a future reader may assume it carries the styling and remove the utilities. One comment, or drop the hook and assert on the utilities.
